lessons.title: What is observability?
learn: Define observability as a property of dependable software, not a tool category
Explain cardinality and dimensionality with numbers
Contrast the three pillars model with the unified storage model, and say when each is right
picture: Kálmán coined observability in 1960 for control theory: can you infer a system's internal state from the outputs you measure? If the information was never captured, nothing recovers it later.

The authors now treat observability as a property of software dependability, next to Laprie's six (availability, reliability, maintainability, safety, confidentiality, integrity). Their seventh: the ability to understand or debug any system state, including ones you've never seen.

Two telemetry models collide. The three pillars store metrics, logs and traces in separate silos. That's right for infrastructure and third-party code you can't change. The unified model stores one wide, structured event (or span) per unit of work in a columnar store and aggregates at read time. That's right for code you write.
deeper: Monitoring tells you up/down and maybe where it's slow. You still need why. Cloud-era failures are mostly partial: slowness with no smoking gun.
Qualitative test of how observable you are: do you detect faults before customers do, can you triage without an alert storm, and can any engineer (not only seniors) find why?

Six principles of the unified model: context makes data combinatorially more valuable; details identify; pre-aggregation is one-way; you don't know what you don't know; static dashboards have limited value; fast feedback loops are everything.
Dimensionality maths: 4 fields → 15 combinations, 8 → 255, 30 → about 1.1 billion (2^n − 1). Adding a 30th field adds as much as the first 29 together.
With AI writing code and agents acting in production, telemetry becomes the last line of defence for checking that code does what was intended.

One checkout request in three silos: metrics give only fleet aggregates (48,291 requests, P99 380 ms, 0.3% errors), logs give five timestamped lines, and the trace shows where the 142 ms went (89 ms in the cart query). No silo links them to this user or build.
names: AWS Well-Architected reliability pillar is the closest framing
One wide structured event per request/hop
lessons.interview: Observability is how well you can explain any state of your system, even a brand-new one, from the telemetry it already emits, without shipping new code. Practically, that means wide, high-cardinality events you can slice at read time. Pre-aggregated metrics can't do that.
aws: Three pillars on AWS: CloudWatch Metrics + CloudWatch Logs + X-Ray, joined by hand
Unified on AWS: OTel/ADOT wide spans → a columnar store (ClickHouse, Athena/Parquet on S3, or a vendor)

practice.q: Your dashboards are green but support reports slow checkouts. What does that tell you, and what would you change?
practice.a: It's a fault-detection gap. Aggregates are averaging away a cohort. I'd move checkout onto wide events with build ID, flags, region, plan and user ID, then compare the slow requests against the baseline. I'd also put an event-based SLO on checkout latency so customer pain pages us, not CPU.

checks.q: A Status column holding only true/false has cardinality…
checks.why: Cardinality is the number of distinct values: two.

checks.q: Which is the authors' main reason three pillars fails for code you write?
o: Relationships between fields are destroyed at write time
checks.why: Splitting by signal type and pre-aggregating loses the cross-field context you need to explain novel problems.

takeaways: Observability is a property you build in, not a product you buy
High cardinality is the point, not a problem
Three pillars for infra; unified wide events for your own code

lessons.title: How code crosses over into production
learn: Explain durable vs disposable code and why maintenance sets the cost of software
Walk through practices 0–5 of the test-in-prod flywheel
Explain why canaries fail without precise observability, and how to fix it
picture: Deploys aren't a switch from dev to ops. They're a process of building confidence, and they should be boring.

Durable code changes in small diffs against a baseline you trust, because its commitments live only in the code. Disposable code is regenerated instead of maintained. When disposable code becomes load-bearing, treat it as durable: tests, review, instrumentation, SLOs.

Six practices form a flywheel. 0: rich data and precision tooling. 1: a dev-to-prod feedback loop. 2: tests before deploy. 3: instrument and validate in prod. 4: separate deploys from releases with feature flags. 5: progressive delivery and automated rollbacks. Everything depends on practice 0.
deeper: Critical path compass: frequency, criticality, visibility, blast radius. Code is scaffolding, a post office (rare but core, like payroll) or a cathedral (constant, carries the business). Anything that can take down critical code is critical too.
The closer code is to writing bits to disk, the more cautious you should be. Persistence mistakes can be permanent.
Practice 1 gold standard: instrument as you write, autodeploy, then look at your change through that instrumentation before you forget what you meant it to do.
Tests stop known problems from recurring. The bar: the only bugs you find in production are new ones. Expect more property-based, behavioural and characterization tests.
Deploy is engineering's job; release is a product or marketing decision. One changeset per deploy. Batching 20 people's changes makes a breaking deploy about 20 times more likely.

Canary failure story: fine at 1%, then every request queued on one DB row lock at 70%. Fix it in two ways: make every failure a new automated health check, and validate intent by comparing cohorts (new build vs old, one endpoint, one plan). That catches a 40% regression at 1% traffic.
Bonus tools: capture/replay for DB upgrades, traffic splitters that diff old vs new APIs, strangler fig migrations.
Critical-path stakes range from 'a newspaper headline tomorrow' to '$20 million lost per minute of delay at market open' to 'someone could die'. Effort should match.
names: CodeDeploy deployment configs; ALB weighted target groups
Columnar options for local trace analysis
Lets agents query telemetry from IDE/chat
lessons.interview: I treat deploy and release as separate. Every merge auto-deploys behind a flag to a canary. I validate intent by comparing the canary cohort against the baseline on the exact endpoint and user tier I changed. Rollbacks are automatic, but only as trustworthy as the signal that triggers them.
aws: Flags: AWS AppConfig feature flags
Progressive delivery: CodeDeploy canary/linear, Argo Rollouts on EKS
Validation: CloudWatch Application Signals or a wide-event store grouped by deploy.build_id

practice.q: Your canary at 1% looked healthy, but the outage started at 70%. Why, and what would you change?
practice.a: Aggregate canary dashboards hide small, threshold and contention effects: lock contention, thundering herds, retries, unrepresentative samples, data corruption. I'd compare canary vs baseline per endpoint and cohort with high-cardinality data, step through more stages, and turn this failure into an automated health check so it can't happen the same way twice.

checks.q: Practice 0 in the flywheel is…
checks.why: Every other practice depends on a precise signal.

checks.q: Why one changeset per deploy?
o: Ownership, a short predictable interval, and easy isolation of a bad change
checks.why: Batching many people's changes multiplies breakage and slows rollback and debugging.

takeaways: Flags + precise observability are worth more than the sum of the parts
A rollback is only as trustworthy as its trigger
terms: Code maintained in place via small diffs; commitments live in the code
Shipping an artifact vs changing user experience
Test that locks in current behaviour to protect expectations

lessons.title: Origins of observability in software
learn: Tell the history briefly: DTrace, Scuba, Honeycomb, vendor rebranding
Recite the six functional requirements
Explain known-unknowns vs unknown-unknowns with the finance analogy
picture: Charity Majors tells the story. Using Scuba at Facebook (while working on Parse) made novel problems findable without prior knowledge, and junior engineers started out-debugging experts. Honeycomb (2016) tried to rebuild that experience from first principles.

They defined observability technically: understand any state, even a never-seen one, which needs high cardinality, high dimensionality, an explorable interface and trace views. Vendors rebranded monitoring between 2019 and 2021, and by the time Gartner added the category in 2022 the word meant anything.

Monitoring is your personal bank account: autopay and a balance check. Observability is running a bank: trace any transaction across millions of accounts, on demand. It costs more because it does more.
deeper: Six functional requirements: (1) wide events per unit of work, ideally hundreds of fields; (2) high cardinality, unique IDs welcome; (3) raw storage, read-time aggregation, all keys fast; (4) zoom from one request to the whole system and see traces; (5) exploratory UI not static dashboards; (6) queries return in seconds.
Traditional tools handle known-unknowns. Observability handles unknown-unknowns, and also product quality and how users actually behave.
Observability 1.0 (a tool per signal, correlations maintained by hand, data paid for many times) vs 2.0 (one store, pay once). Hazel Weakly proposed lakehouse as 3.0.
Cost argument: Gartner says 10–20 observability tools is the norm, so you pay 10–20x per request. Observability is 20–30% of infra spend at many companies.
AI moved the bottleneck from writing code to understanding it.
In 2010 the typical stack was LAMP (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP), and monitoring plus dashboards worked. By 2026 there's no typical stack, and agents add nondeterminism.
names: In-memory event analytics that inspired Honeycomb
Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP stack (2010 norm)
lessons.interview: Monitoring answers questions you predicted. Observability answers ones you didn't, because it keeps raw, high-cardinality events and aggregates at query time in seconds.
aws: Lakehouse-style observability: OTel → Firehose → S3 (Parquet/Iceberg) → Athena; or Amazon Managed Grafana on top

practice.q: An exec says 'we already have observability: we bought tool X.' How do you respond?
practice.a: I'd ask outcome questions. Can any engineer answer a new question in under a minute? Can we group by user ID or build ID without cardinality limits? Do we find issues before customers do? If not, we bought monitoring with a new label. Then I'd show it with a concrete question we can't answer today.

checks.why: Pre-aggregation is a one-way trip; aggregate at read time instead.

checks.why: By then the term had lost its technical meaning.

lessons.title: Getting started with instrumentation
learn: Explain auto vs custom instrumentation and why you need both
Build a custom instrumentation strategy from critical user journeys
Compare head and tail sampling and their failure modes
picture: Instrumentation is code you add so your app reports what it's doing. Without it, you add log lines after the incident and wait for it to happen again.

OpenTelemetry separates the API in your code from the destination in config. The API does nothing until it's configured, so library authors can call it safely. Auto-instrumentation gives you the skeleton (HTTP, DB, RPC calls). Custom instrumentation adds the muscle: business logic, domain errors, user context.
The engineers who write the code should own its instrumentation. A platform team supplies conventions, libraries and review guidelines. Treat instrumentation as a deliverable, like tests.
deeper: Start custom instrumentation from critical user journeys: registration, search, cart and checkout for e-commerce. Capture domain errors such as 'insufficient inventory', and tag them temporary or permanent, actionable or not.
Ask: which users are affected? What are the key pipeline stages? Which flags were on? Then add why-context: segment, active flags, request source.
Auto-instrumentation can drown you. In production, spans for every DB or Redis call can cost real performance. Customising means taking away too.
Write instrumentation backend-agnostic and leave processing (drop, transform, PII filtering) to the pipeline. Removing data later is easier than wishing you'd captured it.
Hidden costs: 10–15 tools means cognitive overload and slower incidents, plus time spent working out why spans were sampled, and cross-AZ egress when you self-host.

Metrics are a form of sampling (pre-aggregation). Head sampling at 1% will probably miss an error that happens 0.1% of the time, and it can't know a downstream call will fail. Tail sampling buffers the whole trace before deciding.
names: Decide at trace start vs after the whole trace
X-Ray sampling rules vs ADOT tail_sampling
lessons.interview: I use auto-instrumentation for coverage and custom instrumentation for the business: journeys, domain errors, user and flag context. I sample everything, and use tail sampling so errors and slow traces are always kept.
aws: ADOT Collector as agent (DaemonSet) + gateway
X-Ray for traces, or export OTLP to a vendor

practice.q: Head sampling at 1% on a service doing 10k req/min. A rare error affects 0.1% of requests. What happens, and what do you do?
practice.a: About 10 errors a minute, and roughly 0.1 of them gets kept, so they're mostly invisible and the downstream outcome isn't known at decision time. I'd switch to tail sampling at a gateway (keep every error and slow trace, sample the rest consistently by trace ID), and record the sample rate on each event so counts can be rebuilt.

checks.q: OTel's API with no SDK configured…
o: Is a no-op with no overhead
checks.why: So library authors can instrument safely.

checks.q: Best starting point for custom instrumentation?
checks.why: They're what the business needs to work.

lessons.exercise: Pick one journey in your system. List its start/end points, five context attributes and three domain errors to capture.
takeaways: Sample everything, but tail-sample what matters

Keep/drop decided at the start of a trace
Decision after buffering the whole trace

lessons.title: Structured events are the building blocks
learn: Show metrics, logs and traces are all structured events
Explain the average-of-averages trap and how histograms fix it
Name the five fields a span needs and how context propagates
picture: A structured event is a flat set of key-value pairs describing one unit of work. Think of a database row.

Metrics (born with SNMPv1 in 1988) are numbers plus tags, aggregated into time buckets. They're cheap and predictable but lossy. Logs are text built for humans; structure them and they become events. Traces are 'fancy logs plus passing IDs around'.
So capture one wide event and derive the metric, the log narrative or the trace when you need it. 'When you pre-decide the shape, you pre-decide the investigation.'
deeper: Counters add up (112 + 78 = 190). Gauges keep the last value. Averages don't combine: per-instance averages of 120/230/200 ms naively give 183 ms, but with counts of 100/57/98 the true average is about 175 ms. A histogram (count + sum) has to be set up before you need it.
Structured log vs structured event: same thing. The only difference is whether your store treats it as structured data or a string.
Span fields: trace ID, span ID, parent ID (absent at the root), start timestamp, duration. Plus service name, span name and attributes.
Propagation: explicit ctx in Go, thread-locals in Python/Ruby, AsyncLocalStorage in Node.
From one span you can compute P99 per minute with PERCENTILE_DISC, add region to GROUP BY with no schema change, use t-digest or HDR histograms for streaming, and stitch traces by trace ID.
lessons.interview: A trace is just structured logs that share a trace ID and point at their parent. If I store wide events, I can derive any metric, including P99 by region, after the fact. Pre-aggregated metrics can't be un-aggregated.
aws: Logs Insights: `stats pct(duration_ms,99) by bin(1m), region` over JSON events
X-Ray segments = spans

practice.q: Three instances report average latency 120, 230 and 200 ms. Your manager says the service average is 183 ms. Respond.
practice.a: That's an average of averages. It's only right if every instance served the same number of requests. With counts of 100, 57 and 98 the weighted mean is 44,710 / 255 ≈ 175 ms. Fix it by emitting histograms (count + sum), or better, raw events, so you can compute it any way later.

checks.q: Which field is absent on a root span?
checks.why: No parent means root.

checks.q: A gauge combined over an interval keeps…
checks.why: Gauges represent a current level.

lessons.title: Making structured events arbitrarily wide
learn: List the attribute families a mature wide event carries
Explain why key timings go on the main span, not only child spans
Use exception.slug and main=true conventions
picture: Jeremy Morrell (Cloudflare) walks through what goes on a wide event. A well-instrumented service has hundreds of attributes.

The families: service and infra metadata, build info, feature flags, runtime/library versions, HTTP and route details, timings and async rollups, errors, user and customer, rate limits, caching, localization, uptime, system metrics, and the domain fields only your business has.

Design events for the queries you'll run. If a slow auth step is only a child span, you need a self-join to group it by user type and region. Put auth.duration_ms on the main event and it's one GROUP BY.
deeper: Build info answers 'did something just deploy?': service.version, git hash, PR URL, diff URL, deployment trigger (merge, Slack bot, config change), deployment.age_minutes.
A version breakdown showed a 500 spike during deploy came entirely from v1. The old version wasn't shutting down cleanly.
Heatmaps reveal bimodal DB query counts and a few N+1 outliers that percentile lines hide.
exception.slug is a unique, greppable literal per throw site. It's low-cardinality and jumps you to the code. A failed request without a slug shows a gap in error handling.
Customer fields matter most. One account can be 10%+ of revenue. Also record impersonation (user.assumed, assumed_by) for audit.
Use uptime_sec_log_10 so crash loops show up next to long-running instances. Cached system metrics on events are fine for debugging, but never alert on them.
Mark wide events with main=true. Otherwise error rates double-count child spans that carry http.response.status_code.
names: ECS task ARN / Lambda request id
lessons.interview: My main span per request carries everything needed to group without joins: build, flags, route, user tier, key timings, DB/HTTP call counts, a greppable error slug. Child spans are for the waterfall; the wide event is for analysis.
aws: Resource attributes from ADOT resourcedetection (ec2, ecs, eks)
Build info injected via CodeBuild env vars into OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES

practice.q: An enterprise customer complains about being rate-limited. With wide events, how do you investigate in five minutes?
practice.a: Filter to their user.id/org.id, then do a heatmap of ratelimit.remaining grouped by http.route. If they suddenly hammered one endpoint, check user agent and source IP: buggy automation or leaked credentials. Then share ratelimit.limit and reset_at with them.

checks.q: Why mark wide events main=true?
o: So aggregate queries don't double-count child spans
checks.why: Child spans also carry status codes.

checks.q: Where should alerts on CPU/memory come from?
checks.why: Span-carried metrics are only sampled when traffic flows.

lessons.title: Instrumenting with OpenTelemetry
learn: Decide when to create a span (interesting + aggregable)
Trace streaming, fan-out, long jobs, serverless and eBPF cases
Layer signals deliberately and keep telemetry consistent with schemas
picture: OTel is trace-first: context is the glue. Interprocess propagation (W3C TraceContext headers, baggage) and intraprocess propagation (scopes, thread-locals) mean any metric or log can be tied to the request that produced it.

Create a span when the work is interesting (it affects latency or failure) and aggregable (grouping by its name gives useful trends). HTTP handlers, DB queries, external calls, cache lookups and queue publish/consume: yes. Helpers, getters, loop iterations: no. A hundred 2 ms spans is too many.

Layer signals rather than duplicating them. Traces for causality, metrics for cheap long-term alerting, logs/events for rare or audited things. A span plus a histogram per HTTP request is a common pair.
deeper: Streaming: put context in the message envelope, use producer spans on publish and consumer spans connected by span links (not parent/child), and propagate a hashed correlation ID. Use metrics with exemplars for fleet alerting, e.g. failed/processed per stage and a publish-to-process histogram.
Long jobs: avoid million-child traces. Model each stage as its own trace with links, or write one summary wide event at the end. Don't re-flush the root span; most stores can't update spans.
Serverless: one well-designed span per invocation. On Lambda, emit lightweight events and assemble them in a stateful Collector (stateless tracing).
eBPF via OBI captures HTTP/gRPC traces with no code changes. It fills gaps for legacy services but needs privileges.
Naming: no IDs in names (GET /users/{user.id}), dot.case, units as metadata (http.server.request.duration, not ..._ms).
Schemas with OTel Weaver validate telemetry in CI and generate helpers. Hash PII, use allowlists, and use transform processors.
Agents: plan first, then execute in small steps. Have them write scripts that do the migration ('automate the automation'), diff old vs new telemetry, and check rules into git.
lessons.interview: For Kafka I don't nest consumers under producers. I inject context into the message, make a consumer span linked to the producer, and carry a business correlation ID through every stage. I alert on per-stage counters and publish-to-process histograms with exemplars.
aws: SQS/SNS/Kinesis: propagate traceparent in message attributes
Lambda: ADOT layer or stateless events + Collector extension
EKS: OBI DaemonSet

practice.q: A nightly ETL runs for 6 hours across thousands of supplier files. How do you instrument it?
practice.a: Not one giant trace. Each stage (extract, transform per batch, load) gets its own trace, joined by span links and a run ID. I'd emit progress metrics for live status, and at the end write a summary wide event with counts, failures by supplier and durations. Alerts go on stage failure ratio and runtime vs baseline.

checks.q: A queue consumer span should usually be…
o: Part of the producer trace forever
checks.why: Async hops become new traces joined by links.

checks.q: Correct metric name?
checks.why: Units belong in metadata.

lessons.exercise: Use pocs/02_mini_tracer: add a producer/consumer pair with links and a correlation ID; verify with the test.
takeaways: Layer, don't duplicate; schemas keep humans and AI aligned

lessons.title: Getting started with observability analysis
learn: Run the core analysis loop on a latency spike
Explain how BubbleUp-style automation works
Place AI agents as copilot, commander or caretaker
picture: Debugging from known conditions relies on scar tissue: seniors who know which dashboard to check. Runbooks rarely keep up, because modern systems seldom fail the same way twice.

Debugging from first principles uses the core analysis loop. What are you trying to understand? Visualise the anomaly. Find the dimensions common inside the anomaly but not in the baseline. Filter and repeat until it's explained. Anyone curious can do this.

The brute-force part (diffing every dimension inside vs outside the selection) is what computers are good at. In a real Honeycomb incident, us-east-1a showed up in 98% of slow events vs 17% of baseline: a cloud-provider AZ problem nobody had announced.
deeper: Keep these in a runbook: owner, on-call, escalation, dependencies, entry-point queries. Don't keep a catalogue of failures and fixes. Wrong docs are worse than none, and instrumentation is the best documentation.
Better telemetry alone doesn't stop you debugging from known conditions (tail -f | grep, flipping dashboards). The analysis method matters.

Copilot: you steer (chat with stack traces). Commander: you set goals, the agent uses tools (Claude Code, Cursor). Caretaker: autonomous, e.g. posts three hypotheses when an alert fires. Errors compound as autonomy grows, and humans still own the outcome.
Agents are optimised for confidence. A field called slow_request (true when >300 ms) was read as the cause. A one-line description fixed it.
lessons.interview: I don't start from a guess. I box the anomaly, diff every dimension against the baseline, take the strongest, filter, and repeat. It works on systems I've never seen, and it's automatable.
aws: Athena/Logs Insights: compare `count(*) by field` inside vs outside a time/latency window
DevOps Guru for anomaly hints (not a replacement)

practice.q: Walk me through debugging a P99 spike on a service you don't know.
practice.a: Confirm it on a heatmap and box the slow band. Compare its dimensions with the baseline: endpoint, build, region, AZ, customer, flags, instance type. Take the most over-represented value, filter, and repeat until a combination explains it. Then pull an exemplar trace to see where the time goes, and only then open code or a profiler.

checks.why: That's the diff step.

lessons.title: Observability-driven development
learn: Contrast TDD and ODD
Use observability as the telescope that aims the debugger
Set AI instrumentation guidelines
picture: TDD checks behaviour against a spec in a controlled, mocked world. ODD checks behaviour against reality. Production varies in ways tests strip out.

Observability works at the scale of systems, not functions. It narrows the search (which component, hop, cohort, build) and then you pick up a debugger or profiler. 'The telescope that aims the microscope.'
Every PR should answer: how will I know this is working as intended? Page the merger for 30–60 minutes after their deploy so they own the outcome.
deeper: Two paths from one latency spike: (a) trace a slow request, timeouts start at service3, reproduce locally with that context; (b) only write endpoints are slow, only some DB primaries, one instance type/AZ, so it's infrastructure, not code.
In microservices the slowness could be code, a usage change, DB capacity, connection limits, the load balancer, service discovery, or a mix.
Four questions after a deploy: is it doing what I expected, how does it compare with the last version, are people using it, is anything odd emerging?

Teams that can't reason about production treat it as a glass castle and roll back by reflex. Accelerate showed speed and quality improve together. North Star metric: lead time to production. Cut batching. Put experienced engineers on the deploy pipeline.

AI writes OTel easily but invents attributes and duplicates signals. Put explicit rules in agent config: spans are primary, attributes on root spans, layer don't duplicate, required route attributes with their sources. Honeycomb saw AI-coauthored commits 3.4x longer with 5.5x net impact.
lessons.interview: Tests tell me my code matches my assumptions. Observability tells me whether production agrees. I ship with the instrumentation that answers 'is it working?', and look while the intent is fresh.
aws: Deploy notifications to the merger via CodePipeline → EventBridge → Slack with a link to a pre-filtered query

practice.q: Your team rolls back by reflex at any blip. How do you change that?
practice.a: Reflex rollbacks come from not being able to tell a real regression from noise. Ship smaller changes behind flags, add canary-vs-baseline views per endpoint, and route post-deploy alerts to the author for an hour. Track lead time and change failure rate. Confidence grows as the signal improves.

checks.q: ODD verifies behaviour against…
checks.why: TDD covers the spec.

checks.q: AI-coauthored commits at Honeycomb were on average…
checks.why: 607 vs 178 lines.

lessons.title: AI agents for observability
learn: Explain why natural-language querying alone fails
Name proven agent use cases
Design the context layer agents need
picture: Boris Tane argues it all comes down to context. An agent with telemetry access can run a multistep investigation. In the book's example: alert, error-rate query, slow traces, correlated logs, then the codebase, ending with a 2 s retry timeout against a 5 s upstream SLA.

Without context, agents struggle. They don't know what they don't know. Naming is chaotic (user-service vs users-svc vs legacy-user-api). The data surface is huge. They confuse correlation with causation.

Proven uses: the first 15 minutes of incident groundwork, explaining traces (that waterfall is an N+1 from an ORM), raising instrumentation quality as code is written, auditing alerts, and proposing data-grounded SLOs.
deeper: Six context layers: service topology, naming conventions and aliases, deployment context, known issues, recent incidents (last 30 days), business context (revenue-critical endpoints, thresholds).

lessons.title: SLOs for reliability
learn: Explain why threshold alerts cause fatigue
Define helpful alerts and event-based SLIs
Roll out SLOs in an organisation; use LLMs to draft them
picture: Alerts on CPU over 80% are potential-cause signals: maybe a backup, GC, or a circuit breaker. Teams learn to ignore them, which is normalization of deviance (a term from the Challenger investigation). Every postmortem then adds more.

Thresholds only cover known-unknowns. Distributed systems are mostly unknown-unknowns: cascading retries, partial brownouts, cache eviction churn. A helpful alert reliably means user experience is degraded, and it can be acted on systematically.
SLOs alert on symptoms of user pain (the what). Observability explains the why. Prefer event-based SLIs (each request good or bad) over time-based ones (each minute good or bad).
deeper: Event SLI example: eligible = POST /checkout, not kube-probe, root span; good = status < 400 and duration ≤ 4 s; ineligible events return null.

Mat Vine (ANZ Bank) got launch-ready in 12 weeks against his 12–18 month estimate. Early standardised OTel with domain conventions removed weeks of regex work. They picked fewer than five user journeys. He's sceptical of piloting on a high-performing team (they rarely need SLOs) and targets stressed, critical teams. Full SDLC integration with hundreds of journeys still took 18 months.

LLMs solve the blank page. Ask for a target with business context and the rationale, then push back. For $1M/month checkout: 99.99% ≈ 4.3 min/month ≈ $100 at risk, vs 99.9% ≈ 43 min ≈ $1,000. Don't out-SLO your dependencies.
Check generated SLIs: models missed the root-span filter. Keep prompts in version control. Imperfect SLOs for many teams beat perfect ones for a few.
Known-unknowns you can alert on: disk 95% full, queue depth over 70%, a TLS certificate expiring in 10 days, error rate over 10% for five minutes.
When challenged on cost, the open-weights model revised five nines down to 99.95% (about 42 minutes a year, under $1k lost on ~$12M/yr). Pushing back on the first answer is part of the method.

I'd start at 99.9% measured on events, then tighten with data.

lessons.title: Acting on SLO burn alerts
learn: Compute error budgets and burn projections by hand
Compare threshold, relative and predictive burn alerts
Explain why event-based SLIs beat time-sliced ones
picture: An error budget is how much failure the business tolerates. 99.9% is about 43 minutes a month, or a count of allowed bad events. Burn alerts forecast exhaustion so you act before the budget is gone. They work best up to about 99.95%.
Use a trailing 30-day window. Fixed calendar windows reset abruptly, while customers' memories don't. 90 days is too long: you could burn 90% of the budget in a day and still technically pass.

Predictive alerts project a baseline window forward. The rule of thumb: extrapolate at most 4x (the last hour predicts 4 hours; the last 6 hours predict 24). Run several lookaheads and act on whichever fires.
deeper: Threshold-crossing (alert at 30% left) just moves the goalpost and causes needless feature freezes.
Relative burn: 10M req/month at 99.9% allows 10,000 failures. That's 2,880 fifteen-minute windows, so about 3.4 per window. A 4x alert fires past about 13 failures, 20x past about 68.
Linear vs proportional: 25 of 50 units failing in a quiet 6 hours. Linear projects 100 more (fine). Proportional projects 50% of a normal day's 1,440 = 720 against a 438 budget, so page now.
Context-aware alerts use the whole window (26 days of history plus 4 projected). They're expensive: Honeycomb's SLO evaluation hit over $5k a day in Lambda until they added caching.

Time-sliced SLIs: if 94% of a minute's requests are under 300 ms, the whole minute is bad, about a quarter of a 4.38-minute four-nines budget. Event-based counts only the 6%. A 1% brownout at 99.99% behaves like a full outage at 99%: more than 7 hours of runway.
Events let you backfill SLI changes and jump from a burning SLO straight to the failing requests.
Lookahead examples: a regression trending 99.9% → 99.88% over a month can wait for the next business day; trending to 98% within an hour pages someone now.
Short-term linear example: 50 failures in the last day projects 400 more over 8 days, 450 in total, which beats the 438 budget, so exhaustion in about 8 days.
Context-aware example: the budget was 65% remaining when the one-day baseline began and 35% now. Burning 30% a day exhausts it well within the 4-day lookahead, so alert.
Read the burn pattern before acting: a gradual steady burn (e.g. 51.4% left), bursts (31.4% left), or one big drop (down to 1.3%) point to different kinds of failure.
lessons.interview: Sliding 30-day window, event-based SLI, two predictive burn alerts: a short one (1h baseline, 4h lookahead) that pages, and a long one (6h baseline, 24h lookahead) that files a ticket. I extrapolate proportionally to expected traffic, not raw counts.

lessons.title: Storage: Honeycomb's Retriever
learn: State the storage requirements for observability
Explain why TSDBs, NoSQL and row stores fall short
Describe Retriever's segments, columns, query path, tiering and durability
picture: Requirements: answers in seconds; every field queryable at full resolution; no privileged dimension except time (and tenant/service); fresh data within seconds; durable and fault-tolerant, even when your own infrastructure is failing.

TSDBs explode on cardinality, since every unique tag combination is a new series. NoSQL needs indexes on everything. Scuba used RAM: about $5k/TB vs under $50/TB for SSD. Bigtable-style row stores need compaction, and Dapper's indexes on just three fields were 76% the size of the data.

Retriever's hybrid: append-only segments per tenant, closed at 1 hour, 250k rows or 1 GB, with min/max timestamps for pruning. Inside each segment, one file per column, scanned row-at-a-time and aggregated per segment, then merged into a top-K.
deeper: Encodings: dictionary, sparse/presence bitmaps, run-length, delta, roaring bitmaps for booleans, IDs as integers, then LZ4 (decompression speed matters more than ratio).
Avoid one-off columns like timestamp_2025…. Use a key/value instead.
Read-time calculated fields: COALESCE($session.id, $session_id) for renames; regex extraction for legacy logs.
Trace lookup is just WHERE trace_id = X. Joins work only within a trace (same partition), using a sliding memory window.
Freshness: queries can force-flush open column files. Ingest and query share only the filesystem.
Closed segments go to S3. Queries fan out over Lambda in a MapReduce style. When 90% have answered, the slow 10% are re-issued and the first copy back wins.
Kafka gives an ordered, durable buffer. Stateless receivers feed deterministic indexers, which can be replayed from an offset.
Scale (Nov 2025): about 1.5 PB, over 1B segments, 3–5M spans/s ingested, median query 50 ms, P99 5 s.
Complex aggregates need sketches: t-digest for percentiles like P99, HyperLogLog for COUNT DISTINCT.
Other columnar engines used for observability: ClickHouse, Google BigQuery, Apache Druid. Observe Inc. built on Snowflake (great for warehousing, less interactive).
lessons.interview: Partition by time into append-only segments, store each field as its own column, prune by time, read only referenced columns, aggregate per segment in parallel, merge, top-K. Tier closed segments to object storage and hedge slow reads.
aws: S3 for segments; Lambda for map; EC2 Graviton for ingest/query; MSK for Kafka
DIY equivalent: Parquet on S3 partitioned by hour + Athena

practice.q: Design storage for 3M spans/s with arbitrary GROUP BY in seconds.
practice.a: Kafka ingest, partitioned by trace ID. Indexers write time-bounded segments with one compressed column file each, dictionary-encoded. Recent segments stay on SSD and can be queried open; closed ones go to S3. Queries prune by time, then fan out over serverless workers, aggregate per segment, merge and top-K, with stragglers hedged. No indexes except time.

lessons.title: Storage: ClickHouse
learn: Explain MergeTree, granules and the sparse primary index
Tune schema: primary key, Map vs JSON, skip indexes, projections, materialized views
Scale with replication, sharding and SharedMergeTree
picture: ClickHouse is an open-source columnar DBMS, a single binary where every node can read and write. MergeTree writes one immutable sorted part per insert and merges parts in the background. A sparse primary index stores the first key of each ~8,192-row granule.

A query prunes partitions, then parts (by min/max key), binary-searches the sparse index to find granules, reads only the filter columns, then fetches output columns for matching rows (lazy materialisation). Observability data often compresses 10–20x or more.
Choose the primary key to match how you query: (ServiceName, Timestamp) if you filter by service first. Put hot attributes in real columns, everything else in a Map or the newer JSON type.
deeper: Caches: query result cache (by AST), query condition cache (a bit per granule per predicate), filesystem cache, userspace page cache.
Ingest via the OTel Collector exporter. Prefer fewer, bigger inserts (a batch processor at a gateway) or async_insert=1. Inserts are idempotent by block hash, so retries are safe.

ASOF JOIN connects events at query time with no trace IDs, e.g. container crash to the next ContainerReady gives recovery seconds (nginx 961 s, apiserver 63 s), and per image tag that's MTTR by version.
Skip indexes: bloom_filter on RequestId (0.1% false positives), bloom on map keys/values, tokenbf_v1 for message tokens, MinMax for outliers. Only worth it when few granules match.

Projections: hidden copies re-sorted by a different key, chosen automatically. Incremental materialized views: insert triggers that route error logs to a table and aggregate them for alerting. Merge tables give one view over evolving schemas.
TTL: move to S3 at 90 days, delete at 365. Use ttl_only_drop_parts or weekly partitions so it stays cheap.

Scale vertically first. Replication via Keeper (Raft) is active-active and eventually consistent (insert_quorum when you need it). Sharding via Distributed tables. Multi-region: shard by region. SharedMergeTree separates storage from compute.
Sizing: 32 cores/128 GB ≈ 20B events/day, peaking at 300–400k/s. 20 TB raw/day becomes 1–2 TB on disk.
Example 14-4 result: /api/v1/orders served 40,723 requests with P95 1.034 s and P99 1.78 s, the obvious first target. Grouping by path × version × IP would be impossible as metrics.
Two servers with 7.5 TB NVMe each (full copies for HA) hold about three days of data before object storage. Load-balancing writes across replicas reaches about 500k events/s.
Replication uses the ReplicatedMergeTree engine; Map columns typically use CODEC(ZSTD(1)).
lessons.interview: ClickHouse is good here because parts are immutable and sorted with a sparse index, so time+service queries skip almost everything, and columns not referenced are never read. I evolve the schema with materialised columns, projections and materialised views as query patterns emerge.
aws: ClickHouse Cloud on AWS or self-managed on EC2 with NVMe (i4i/i7ie) + S3 tier
Alternative: Athena/Iceberg for cold, OpenSearch for search-heavy logs

practice.a: Map lookups read every key and value. If pod_name is hot, materialise it as a real column (or let the JSON type do it) and add a bloom or set skip index if values cluster by primary key. If it's a primary access path, add a projection ordered by it. Then check with system tables that granules are actually being skipped.

lessons.title: Cheap and accurate enough sampling
learn: Reconstruct counts and percentiles from sampled data
Implement consistent sampling for traces
Choose per-key, target-rate, head, tail or buffered sampling
picture: Most events are identical successes. Keep representative good events and every interesting bad one, record the sample rate on each kept event, and rebuild true counts by weighting.

Constant probability (1 in N) is easy, and P50/P99 survive unchanged. It fails when errors matter more than successes, when some customers are 100x louder than others, or when a surge could flood the backend.

Trace decisions must be consistent. Derive the decision from the trace ID so every service keeps or drops the same trace. Head sampling decides with what's known at the start; tail sampling buffers the whole trace (needs a collector); buffered approaches combine both.
deeper: Dynamic rates break simple multiplication, so use weights: median of values {1,3,7} with rates {5,2,9} is 7, not 3.
Per-key rates (status, method, customer). Per-key + recent volume (e.g. [customer, dataset, error] counts in the last 30 s). Target-rate (N events/s). Per-key target rates (dynsampler-go).
Errors and slow requests (>500 ms) get their own budget. Ordinary ones are rate-limited.
Parents pass the head decision and rate to children. A Redis child sampled at 1/1000 never orphans when its parent is 1/10.
Strategy depends on traffic shape: a front page (90% identical), a DB proxy (repeated patterns), a service behind a cache (mostly unique).
names: Go library for dynamic per-key sampling
lessons.interview: I sample by key with target rates: errors and slow requests are always kept, noisy successes are squeezed, and health checks never kept. The rate travels on every event so counts and percentiles can be rebuilt. Trace decisions hash the trace ID so traces stay whole.

practice.q: Why put sample_rate on every event instead of configuring it in the backend?
practice.a: Rates change: dynamically, per key, per service, at runtime. Only a rate attached to the event tells the backend how many events each one stands for. That lets you rebuild counts, sums and percentiles correctly even when rates vary.

lessons.title: Telemetry pipelines
learn: Name the pipeline stages and resilience features
Choose agent-only, agent+gateway or multi-tier
Plan a phased migration and make the ROI case
picture: Mike Kelly (Bindplane): treat the flow of telemetry as its own concern. Stages: collect → normalize & secure → enrich → reduce → route, underpinned by resilience and a control plane.

Built on the OTel Collector (receivers, processors, exporters, extensions). The same binary runs as a lightweight agent near workloads and as gateway clusters doing the heavy lifting. Fleets are managed with OpAMP.
Agent + gateway is the default production pattern. Multi-tier (local then regional gateways) suits large estates.
deeper: Normalize to OTLP. Redact PII and enforce residency (GDPR, FedRAMP, HIPAA) before data leaves. Enrich with k8s, business and geo/DNS lookups.
Reduce by filtering, deduplicating, aggregating and sampling. Route by fan-out (SIEM, APM, analytics, archive). Adding a tool becomes a config change.
Resilience: buffers per stage with disk persistence, retries with exponential backoff, backpressure, HA agents and gateways.
Migration: start greenfield, then redirect existing agents to gateways, then replace them. Fragile legacy can stay in phase 2.
Evidence: 20–40% of SIEM data is never queried. One customer had 25,000+ collectors drifting. Savings of 50%+ are common; one customer avoided a $2.6M overage. Save 50%, reinvest 10%, net about 40%.
lessons.interview: I'd put a Collector gateway tier between apps and backends. It redacts PII once, enriches, samples and routes. That removes vendor coupling and lets security and observability share one clean stream. Agents stay light; gateways scale horizontally with queues.

lessons.title: Ontologies for humans and AI
learn: Explain semantic failure vs infrastructure failure
Define nouns, invariants and provenance for a domain

picture: Frank Chen opens at 2 a.m.: the infrastructure dashboard is green and bills are wrong. Nothing is broken in code. The failure is in meaning. 'Availability' means server up, low latency, or a correct bill, depending on who you ask.

An ontology maps a domain's nouns, relationships and rules, and becomes real through semantic conventions. In the example: IntervalSeries (usage) + Tariff (rules) → BillSet (output); ActionPlan is the AI's untrusted proposal.

Invariants (coverage, arithmetic, determinism) become runtime assertions, a semantic firewall. In the AI sandwich, deterministic logic wraps the AI: simulate every proposal and reject any whose maths doesn't hold.
deeper: Provenance: every BillSet records input_series_id, applied_tariff_id and ruleset_version, so a cost spike can be traced to a data or logic change.
CI gates: deterministic (hash, arithmetic, coverage), simulation (predicted savings reproduce within tolerance), semantic (golden dialogs, confidence floor around 0.6).
Signal parity: CI emits the same JSON as production, so the assertion that blocks a PR is the query that pages.
Signals: structural integrity, logic stability (ranking drift), AI reliability (proposal acceptance and eval pass rate).

Rejected proposals become golden dialogs (PII scrubbed) and block deploys until passed. Eval pass rate is an SLI. In the example, a predicted $20 saving that simulates to $0.50 is logged as rejected/simulation_mismatch.

lessons.title: Observability for CI/CD
learn: Model CI workflows as traces and find the critical path

picture: CI/CD is a production system for developer feedback, and it has the best ROI of any observability work. Every request has a developer waiting on it, and volume is small (about a dozen PRs per developer per day at most).
Workflow = trace, job = spans under it, step = span within the job. Add repo and branch. Your first SLIs are end-to-end time to validated, flake rate (success on retry) and test failure rate on main.
Jobs form a DAG. Only the critical path matters: if Rust dominates, speeding up the Go build changes nothing.
deeper: Experiment instead of guessing: more cores didn't help a webpack build missing ThreadLoaders; Go builds halved with more cores; slow releases were network-bound pushing images to every region from one job.
Retries hide 5% flakes but inflate the tail: P50 stays flat while P90 doubles. Ephemeral dedicated runners can be cheaper once retries are counted. Watch OS limits and cgroups.
Use toolchain caches (Go module/build) for incrementality without losing isolation.

Honeycomb: SLO of no more than 5% of builds over 15 minutes. Median doubled from 7 to 14 minutes (2018–19). PRs per week went from 10–20 to 100+. Amdahl's law bit. Traces showed 3.5 GB gzip-moved between steps, so they switched to a single Docker Bake. BuildKit has native OTel: set TRACEPARENT. Result: under 7 minutes, so developers stay and watch.
Tools: GitHub Actions OTel receiver/action, Buildkite native OTel, otel-cli exec, DOCKER_CLI_OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT.
The common complaint, 'the suite takes 5 minutes on my MacBook but 20 in CI', usually means CI starts from scratch every time. Persist the toolchain caches.

lessons.interview: I trace the pipeline: workflow as a trace, jobs as spans. I find the critical path, set an SLO on time-to-validated, and track flake rate separately so retries don't quietly double the tail.

lessons.title: Mobile and frontend observability
learn: Explain why backend patterns fail on devices
Design local ring buffer + control plane telemetry
Measure UX as intention → outcome and debug by cohort
picture: On devices you inherit the environment: thousands of models and OS versions, flaky networks, captive portals, ad blockers. Telemetry has to respect battery, bandwidth, privacy and cost. The status quo is crash reporting, RUM, CI benchmarks, and a separate product-analytics silo.

It's hard because workflows aren't auto-instrumentable. They span screens and threads with no shared context. Apps can't see the system around them. And telemetry is lost most often exactly when the app is struggling, which biases you toward false calm.

Matt Klein's approach: log everything to an on-device ring buffer that doesn't leave by default, and let a real-time control plane push rules saying what to send and when. Hanson Ho's: measure intention → outcome (checkout completion rate), detect user impact first, then find the app cause by cohort.
deeper: 1% of users at 2x slower may not move P50 or P99. At 100M DAU that's a million people.
Mature apps exceed 99.9% crash-free sessions, so the leverage is in hangs, rage taps and functional bugs. Malformed JSON in a 200 OK can break the golden path while the server reports 99.99%.
Klein's constraints: long release cycles, users who care about data, normal disconnection, unplanned termination, huge cardinality, and the main UI thread.
Control-plane FSM example: on the checkout screen, if the user leaves or 15 s pass without checkout, count it and upload the session replay. You can target a cohort or a single user.
P50 on mobile says little about the tail: a 1 s cold start on a new phone vs 10 s on a nine-year-old one.

FakeBurger findings: Next button below the fold; a new discount-code format disabled Submit on first entry; rare errors hitting heavy users; many small glitches. Watch for adoption bias: early adopters have better phones.

Classic mobile debugging story: NullPointerExceptions across several screens. RUM sessions ending in the crash all show a tap on a button whose label has non-ASCII characters, and a string assumption in that button's code is the bug.
names: Real user monitoring of client events
lessons.interview: On mobile I measure UX as completed intentions (checkout started vs finished), keep rich logs in a local ring buffer, and use server-pushed rules to upload sessions only for the cohorts and conditions I'm investigating. That's cheap, survives bad networks, and targets the tail.

Look for the cohort with an outsized drop, then push a rule to capture session replays for abandoned checkouts in that cohort.

checks.why: Struggling apps can't send, so things look calmer than they are.

lessons.title: Performance engineering
learn: Combine tracing and profiling
Pick compute purchasing models and squeeze fleets with data
Find Kubernetes and serverless cost waste
picture: Honeycomb found load-balancer latency that its traces didn't show. A pprof flame graph showed regexp.Compile using 17% of CPU, because the HTTP router was rebuilt on every request. The fix was five lines, and tracing couldn't have seen it.

Tracing is the forest; profiling shows the tree rings. Account for request time to about 100 ms with spans, then use sampling profilers (about every 10 ms) for function-level detail. Read flame graphs by width (total time) and stacking (call chains). Continuous profiling is cheap because profiles repeat and compress.

Cost: choose compute models (capex, reserved, VMs, spot, Fargate/Cloud Run, Lambda) from load data. Squeeze fleets until the SLO tail degrades. Test new hardware generations and Arm (about 30% better price-performance per generation).
deeper: Kubernetes: use heatmaps rather than percentiles for node saturation. Ingest Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler logs. Watch rollout surges double apparent pod counts (group by template hash), and DaemonSet overhead. Bin-packing: 20-core pods on 32-core nodes strand 11 cores, so use 64-core nodes or 15-core pods.

Serverless: cold-start init is billed, so instrument init, running and sleeping spans. Lambda Power Tuner. S3 reads are about 25% of Retriever's serverless cost. Provisioned concurrency is the worst of both worlds.
Ingest the cost and usage report as wide events. Watch NAT gateway and cross-AZ transfer. Size savings plans from your minimum hourly spend.
Per-customer profiling found protobuf→JSON serialisation repeated per Lambda invocation (fixed by caching) and deeply nested if/else queries (fixed by adding switch).
Brendan Gregg's books are the reference.
Old utilisation rule: run Intel instances with SMT/hyperthreading at about 40% and Arm (no SMT) at 70–80%. Retest on current cores; Arm can run hotter because it isn't contending with itself.

Purchasing models across clouds: reserved (Savings Plans, committed use), VMs (EC2, Azure VMs, GCE), interruptible (Spot, Azure Spot, Google Preemptible), elastic containers (Fargate, Azure Container Apps, Cloud Run), functions (Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Functions), or capex (e.g. Oxide racks).
A minute of profile data is about 5 MB, but two hours isn't 120x that, because stacks repeat and compress well.
names: Two hardware threads per core; contend at high utilisation
lessons.interview: Traces tell me which request and which hop. Profiles tell me which function and line. Linked per span or per customer, I can say what was slow, for whom and why, and fix the 5-line bug instead of buying hardware.
aws: CodeGuru Profiler / Pyroscope
Compute Optimizer; Karpenter on EKS; Graviton
CUR 2.0 → Athena as wide events

practice.q: The cloud bill grew 40% in a quarter with flat traffic. Where do you look?
practice.a: Load the CUR into a queryable store and group by service, usage type and tag. Usual culprits: NAT/cross-AZ transfer, idle reserved capacity, oversized requests vs actual pod use, rollout artefacts, a hot loop. Then profile the top-cost services and fix the largest share first: 1% of 10% beats 5% of 1%.

checks.q: Why couldn't tracing find the regexp bug?
o: The tracing hook runs after the router is built
checks.why: The cost happened before the instrumented code.

checks.q: 20-core pods on 32-core nodes waste about…
checks.why: 31 usable minus 20.

checks.q: Why can Arm instances often run at higher utilisation than SMT Intel?
o: No SMT threads contending with each other
checks.why: Retest on current hardware anyway.

lessons.title: Observability for LLM applications
learn: Explain why latency isn't UX for LLM apps
Design LLM telemetry with OTel GenAI conventions
Run the eval ↔ telemetry flywheel
picture: LLMs are opaque (no debugger), nondeterministic (temperature doesn't guarantee repeatability), fed an unbounded input space, and changing fast. Fast but wrong answers don't satisfy users, and in agents one failed tool call matters less than whether the task got done.

Evals are like tests with three outcomes: pass, fail, maybe. Honeycomb's Canvas uses question evals (string-match facts from golden data) and task evals (score the investigation steps). Great evals can still sit alongside bad UX.
The flywheel: production traces become eval cases, evals guide harness and prompt fixes, and the fixes show up in telemetry.
deeper: Follow the OTel GenAI semantic conventions: tokens in/out, model, sampling parameters, prompts on client spans.
Decide how much input/output to store. Link to a system of record rather than inlining large bodies. Mind privacy.
Derive cost at query time from model + tokens; there's no standard cost attribute. Record feedback (thumbs, retries) as attributes.
Put prompt-cache hit info on spans. Track provider rate limits, retries and latency, and use SLOs rather than thresholds for provider failures.
Honeycomb's MCP server SLO was 90% query success. They found calling models guessed field names and mishandled time ranges.
Query Assistant: 25% errors, down to ~14% with harness repairs (e.g. drop the column on COUNT), down to under 1% with prompt work. Then they shipped COUNT-with-column because users clearly wanted it.
is_slow (a calculated field, >500 ms) was misread as a cause until it got a description. Public benchmarks can mislead about your users.
Classic latency economics no longer transfer to AI: Greg Linden's 2006 Amazon result (+100 ms → revenue drop) and Google's (+0.5 s → −20% traffic) assumed speed was the main measure of UX.
lessons.interview: For LLM features I instrument the full harness, not just the model call: tokens, model, prompt version, tool calls, validation repairs and user feedback. I promote bad traces to evals. Cost is derived from tokens at query time so I can compare prompt versions.
aws: Bedrock invocation logging + CloudWatch GenAI observability
Bedrock evaluations; SLOs on model invocation success/latency

practice.q: Your LLM feature errors 25% of the time. Plan?
practice.a: Group errors by type from traces. Validation failures that are nearly right get deterministic repair in the harness. Then improve prompts and tool descriptions against an eval set built from real failing traces. Watch for errors that reveal unmet user needs, and change the product. Set an SLO on success excluding provider timeouts.

checks.q: Possible eval outcomes?
checks.why: Nondeterminism needs a 'maybe'.

checks.q: Recommended way to track LLM cost?
o: Derive at query time from model + tokens
checks.why: Easy to reprice and compare versions.

lessons.title: Case study: Fin
learn: Tie engineering to a customer metric and a business metric
Find the critical path in async agent systems
Use the Rasmussen boundaries to frame observability
picture: Fin (formerly Intercom) charges per resolved conversation, so resolution rate is the north star. It has risen about 1 point a month since March 2023, from dozens of stacked A/B tests. Hundreds of engineers in 20 teams ship about 100 changes a day.

When customers said Fin was slow, component speedups didn't help. They defined time to first token, measured on the frontend, and rebuilt traces with low-level spans showing where control passes between transactions. That revealed the critical path.

Eager requests (start the LLM work in parallel with pre-processing) cut 2 s from median TTFT. But conversations routed to humans wasted that LLM spend, which finance found in a quarterly margin review. Fix: cost per interaction on every trace, with its own SLO.
deeper: Latency is protected with an event-based SLO: percentage of interactions faster than the new baseline. Thresholds were too noisy given model provider variability.
The warehouse query for LLM waste took minutes and refreshed daily: fine for finance, useless for engineers shipping 100 changes a day.

Rasmussen's boundaries: acceptable performance (customers), economic failure (margins), unacceptable workload (engineers). Observability's job is to show operators where they stand against all three, in real time and linked to traces.
The 'last mile' is empathy for customers, the business and engineers. Without it, observability is just a logging-cluster cost.
names: Drift toward failure within three boundaries
Start likely work before it's confirmed
lessons.interview: Pick one customer signal (TTFT) and one business signal (cost per interaction), put both on the same detailed traces, and set SLOs on each. Speed gains that quietly burn margin show up the same day, not the next quarter.
aws: RUM for TTFT; X-Ray/ADOT spans with cost attribute; Application Signals SLOs on both

practice.q: You added speculative LLM calls to cut latency. What could go wrong, and how do you catch it?
practice.a: Wasted work when the speculation isn't used: cost rises without any latency signal, because those paths emit no latency metric. Catch it by putting cost per interaction (including discarded speculative calls) on traces with an SLO, and by tracking the speculation hit rate.

lessons.title: Learning speed is the constraint: letter to CTOs
learn: Name the three sociotechnical debts
Explain why AI amplifies existing behaviour
Measure whether the shift is working
picture: In the AI era, delivery isn't limited by writing code. It's limited by how fast you can validate, understand and learn. Unpaid sociotechnical debt is the biggest drag. AI doesn't remove the need for engineering discipline; it removes the excuses for not having it.

The three debts. Developers live in tests, not reality: only ops has production in its loop. Telemetry is treated as infrastructure, not product: orgs went broad instead of deep. Developer tools were never designed as products: 'add good telemetry' is a maze.
Boris Tane's framing: the old wide SDLC collapses into intent → build → observe → repeat. Observability is the only quality gate that survives, and context is what's left.
deeper: A Gartner reference customer went from $50k/yr on monitoring (2009) to $24M/yr on 'observability' (2024): 48% a year for 15 years. Observability takes 20–30% of infra spend.
Tests: does a Friday shipper know by Monday how it performed? Do incidents take 15 minutes with the rockstar and 45 without? Can a new hire instrument a service without pinging three people?
DORA 2025: AI amplifies whatever you already have, whether strong feedback loops or chaos.
Shifts: match tools to architecture; run observability as a platform product; treat product observability as an investment. Observability inherits the properties of the code it observes.
Measure: time from deploy to validated understanding; share of incidents found internally vs by customers; share of deploys with a post-deploy check.
Darragh Curran (Fin CTO): shipping is your heartbeat; understanding is your breathing.
names: Misalignment of social and technical structures
Product thinking for internal developer tools
lessons.interview: With AI, generating code is cheap and confidence is expensive. I'd invest in the developer-to-production feedback loop and measure time from deploy to validated impact, not dashboard counts.
aws: Platform paved path: ADOT auto-instrumentation via EKS add-on + standard resource attributes + golden queries

practice.q: As a new head of platform, you have one quarter. What do you do about observability?
practice.a: Run three tests: can devs validate a Friday deploy by Monday, does incident resolution depend on specific people, can a new hire instrument a service alone. Pick one critical domain and instrument it deeply. Ship a paved path (library + defaults + golden queries). Report deploy-to-understanding time and the share of incidents found internally.

checks.q: Per DORA 2025, AI…
checks.why: Strong loops compound; chaos compounds too.

checks.q: Which is NOT one of the three debts?
o: Dev tools never designed as products
checks.why: The three are about feedback, telemetry ownership and tooling design.

lessons.title: Systems thinking for software delivery
learn: Explain amplifying vs balancing feedback loops with software examples
Use Meadows' leverage points
Diagnose lossy, laggy, unpredictable, wrong and missing feedback
picture: Software delivery is a sociotechnical system. Trist's principle: optimise the social and technical together. The weakest interventions (budgets, metrics, reorganisations) get absorbed. Changing information flows is far stronger, and observability is an information flow that creates feedback loops.

Amplifying loops become virtuous circles or death spirals: confidence (deploy more, smaller, faster MTTR), learning (answers lead to more questions), quality (clean baseline). Balancing loops need accurate signal to regulate, e.g. how many people join an incident, or observability spend.

What separates a virtuous circle from a death spiral is whether you can see well enough to correct yourself. Two teams breaking up a monolith with the same intent: the one with traces pauses at service eight; the other piles on services until it needs a rewrite.
deeper: Bad feedback: lossy (you double down on a change that hurt 0.5% of users), laggy (a Friday complaint about Tuesday's change, after 40 more changes), unpredictable (ingest gaps teach people to ignore intermittents), wrong (false alerts), missing (open loop: 'don't deploy Fridays').
Workarounds become institutions: CABs, freeze windows, stale runbooks. That's theatrical safety, and standing still is falling behind.

Observability of observability: e.g. checkout makes 60% of trace volume but gets 10% of queries; a dashboard scans 500 GB per load and nobody has opened it in 3 months; adding user_id multiplied cardinality 10,000x; $5k/month of fraud queries caught a $2M incident. Give teams budgets.

Meadows' leverage points (subset, high to low): goals, self-organisation, rules, information flows, amplifying loops, balancing loops. People often push the right lever the wrong way: deploys hurt, so they added CABs and release trains.
lessons.interview: Observability is a leverage point because it changes what people can see, which changes many decisions every day. Without it, confidence loops run backwards: fewer, bigger, scarier deploys.
aws: Observability-of-observability: CUR + vendor usage APIs per team tag; budgets via AWS Budgets

practice.q: Your org banned Friday deploys and added a CAB after two outages. Respond.
practice.a: That's the right lever pushed the wrong way. Slower, bigger batches make failures more likely and harder to diagnose. Fix the feedback instead: smaller deploys behind flags, canary cohort comparison, automated rollback on SLO burn. Then remove the gates once evidence shows lower change failure rate.

lessons.title: The landscape through a systems lens
learn: Contrast dev, ops and value-creation loops
Map three pillars and unified models to the loops they serve
Choose a starting point by bottleneck
picture: Most orgs run a fast but isolated dev loop (build, test, merge, move on) and a slow, reactive ops loop (alert, investigate, fix). Neither connects 'I wrote this' to 'I can see what it did'.
The value loop is build → deploy → observe → learn. Fin ships its Ruby monolith about 70 times a day, 8–15 minutes from merge to full rollout. Deploying without looking is an open loop.
Why closing it is rare: the economics of cognitive load. Without precision data, looking isn't worth it, so nobody looks, so the tools never improve. AI breaks the stalemate.
deeper: Precision means something like: 'for requests on build X with flags Y, test users on the 10% canary vs the 90% baseline, compaction rate for long strings rose 5% and disk use fell 30%; status codes unchanged.' 'No spike in errors' isn't precise.
Three pillars suits operational outcomes and infrastructure. Unified storage suits developer learning: e.g. all EU mobile users with flag X who hit errors in checkout.
AI makes code nearly free; the constraint is coherence. Most code is brownfield or blackfield. Agents can check back on slow burns, and continuous-review agents can flag risky changes.
Most orgs spend on the goalie (ops) and leave the field empty. Decide which loop is your bottleneck before running vendor bake-offs.
lessons.interview: I'd ask which loop is our bottleneck. If it's stability, mature three-pillars tooling is fine. If it's delivery speed or AI-generated code nobody understands, invest in the developer learning loop and unified data.
aws: Ops loop: CloudWatch alarms + Incident Manager
Dev loop: deploy event → pre-filtered cohort comparison link to the author

practice.q: How would you prove to a skeptic that the dev loop matters more than another dashboard?
practice.a: Show the gap: how long after merge before anyone looks at a change, and what share of issues customers find first. Then pilot on one service. Auto-link each deploy to a canary-vs-baseline view and measure how many regressions are caught before customers notice.

lessons.title: The business case
learn: Build separate cases for operational vs developer loops
Use external and internal measures
Frame observability as investment vs cost center correctly
picture: Start with which loop is the bottleneck, not vendor features. The operational loop is a safety net and a cost center: uptime, faster incident response, avoided outages, lower burnout. Fred Hebert's line: great firefighters should start reading the fire codes.

Developer learning loops are an investment. Many productivity tools fail to pay off because they don't close the loop: chaos engineering without attribution is just chaos, flags without validation are a trust fall, progressive delivery without detection is just a slower pipeline.

Observability inherits the properties of the code it observes. Infrastructure observability is a cost center; observability of revenue code is an investment; delivery tooling multiplies your biggest cost, engineers.
deeper: Signs of operational trouble: customers find bugs first, small incidents snowball, the investigation backlog grows, break/fix crowds out features, nobody will ship the AI diffs.

External measures: differentiators and their SLOs. Honeycomb: builder queries under 5 s 85% of the time, deep queries under 30 s 85%, data queryable within 60 s 99.95% of the time, 99.99% durability. Amazon: 100 ms ≈ 1% of sales. Walmart: +2% conversion per second saved. Staples: +10% from a 1 s faster home page.
Pivots found by watching users: Instagram (Burbn), YouTube (dating), Twitter (Odeo), Slack (a game's chat tool).
Internal measures: uncertainty is expensive, and hiring adds coordination tax. Report developer observability into the VP Eng/CTO, not IT/ops, and staff it like a platform team.
Finance-friendly terms: fully loaded engineering cost, capacity recovered from firefighting, time to market. Use conservative baselines.
lessons.interview: I split the case. Ops loop: uptime, MTTR, avoided outages, retention. Dev loop: deploy frequency, batch size, hypothesis-to-validation time, issues found internally. Then I tie each to a business metric the CFO already tracks.
aws: Tag-based cost allocation; observability spend per team via CUR tags

practice.q: Make the 60-second pitch to the CFO for a unified observability platform.
practice.a: Engineering salaries are our biggest cost, and we lose a large share to firefighting and slow validation. Faster validation means fewer regressions, faster releases and less war-room time. We'll measure it by deploy frequency, incidents found before customers, and hours recovered, against a conservative baseline. Infrastructure monitoring stays lean as a cost center.

lessons.title: Diagnosing your observability investment
learn: Answer 'cut observability spend' with a diagnosis
Use loop-specific leading indicators
Apply tiers, attribution and impact statements
picture: Gartner: observability spend has grown at least 40% a year for 15 years. It's the second-largest R&D software line after cloud, typically 10–25% of the infrastructure bill. Don't pay observability prices for monitoring outcomes.
The firefighting trap: if your goalie makes 50 saves a game, your defence isn't working. Cutting spend usually means less data, more blind spots, and higher costs later.
Activities aren't learning. Observability supplies the attribution, validation and detection that turn practices into learning.
deeper: Ops investment is working if: known causes are found faster, alert quality improves, escalations fall, recovery speeds up.

Dev investment is working if: engineers answer novel questions, deploys get more frequent with smaller batches, more people debug, hypothesis-to-validation time shrinks, and more issues are found internally.
Diagnostic questions: what share of spend fights fires vs prevents them? Does it build capabilities that move business metrics? Which feedback mechanism turns each practice into learning?
Actions: cap each investment at diminishing returns, write impact statements, tier telemetry with feature-flagged verbosity (high/medium/low), attribute cost per request and give teams budgets.
names: Full cost of an outage incl. churn, SLA penalties
lessons.interview: When asked to cut, I first show what we buy. Then I tier: rich traces for revenue and active-development services, sampled traces for stable customer-facing ones, health checks for the rest. Every team sees its own spend.

practice.a: It isn't a communication problem. Check tool fit vs loop (are we paying observability prices for monitoring?), instrumentation quality and adoption. Check the leading indicators per loop. Then tier services, kill unqueried data, attribute cost to teams, and reinvest where it changes outcomes.

lessons.title: The organizational shift
learn: Run the five tests for legacy-masquerading-as-modern
Handle resistance from vendors, teams and leadership
Secure a mandate and run the roadmap and team
picture: Rick Clark (UST) argues many orgs have legacy observability wearing a new label. War rooms, manual correlation, the same three people, folklore mysteries.

Five tests. Ownership: how do you know your merge works? Two-or-three people: 60–80% of engineers should investigate alone. Mystery: what weirdness do we just accept? Arbitrary question: answer a never-asked slice in under 60 seconds. Deployment confidence: read-only Fridays and CABs are fear signals.
Change needs a coalition (people who feel the pain, plus the heroes who held things together), a mandate with real authority, and a product-minded roadmap.
deeper: Resistance: the organisational immune response (committees, starved pilots, redefined success) — name it aloud. Vendors are incentivised to sell tiers, AI add-ons and services. Teams are protecting identity ('I'm the Splunk person') and headcount. Leadership carries sunk cost and memories of failed consolidations.
Rick's mistake: bypassing the principal network architect, who controlled IP allocation. Requests that should take hours took weeks until he was brought in.
Pitch it as risk reduction, capability and burden (best engineers spending 30% of their time in war rooms). Not consolidation, not cost savings. Mention open standards and the AI forcing function.

Roadmap: one domain at full depth; paved paths; platform engineering principles (build little, use OTel); rerun the tests at 6 months; expand gradually (budget shifting about 10% in year one to 40% by year three).

Team: platform, SDKs, standards, vendors, DX, not instrumenting every service. Use Wardley's pioneers, settlers and town planners. Turn 'Splunk person' into 'telemetry architect'. Don't promise no jobs change.
lessons.interview: I'd prove the gap with five evidence tests, build a coalition including the legacy experts, get a mandate that new services instrument the new way, and start with one domain instrumented deeply. Success is war rooms stopping and Friday deploys being boring.

lessons.title: Build vs buy vs open source
learn: Apply the build/buy 2×2 and its OSS-aware version
Calculate the hidden cost of 'free'
Spot pricing and lock-in traps; run a buy-and-build platform
picture: Decide which you hate more, your money or your time. Name your biases: engineers want to build (surgeons want to cut), plus sunk cost, not-invented-here, and fear of migration.

Rick Clark's 2×2: business value × ubiquity. Build bespoke differentiators (e.g. Retriever for Honeycomb). Buy commodity, low-value things. Bespoke, low-value things should not exist. Commodity things with high value need a real decision. Peter Corless' version for open source: create, adopt, acquire, avoid, plus commission.
Default for most: buy the platform, build the integration layer. Observability is unusual software: it watches the watchers, so it must not go down with your production stack.
deeper: Should-not-exist example: a bank's custom Apache 1.3 request handler outlived its authors and cost over $10M to unwind once it became a compliance issue.
'Free' ELK: vs an ~$80k/month quote, it actually cost $80k/month in hardware plus three engineers and recruiting, over $2M a year.

Decide-quadrant questions: the job to be done, how unique you really are, the smallest version, product management, timeline, who supports it. Near the disk: battle-tested. Near the UX: custom is fine.
Examples: SLO tooling, buy ~90%. A ~200-line React OTel wrapper, build it (two weeks). Chargeback, use vendor tags plus a script.

Open source is free as in puppies, not beer. Pricing red flags: per-seat, per-host, per-service, per-query models that penalise curiosity. A Gartner customer growing 48% a year for 15 years implies about 358x the cost.
Avoid lock-in: native OTel plus distros, the Collector not vendor agents, written cost models with buffers. The observability team writes libraries, standardises naming, manages vendors and educates.
Caveats: no big vendor sells monitoring at monitoring prices; hyperscalers may build; enterprises need tiers.

Matthew Sanabria (Oxide): use the vendor-neutral OTel Collector, not the vendor agent. Model costs for today and for growth, add a buffer for misconfigurations that spike the bill, and trust nothing that isn't in writing.
If customers are genuinely fine with 98–99.5% availability, self-hosted open source can be much cheaper. Part of what a vendor sells is a stack independent of your own failures.

Promotion incentives drive tech debt: engineers expect to reach principal faster by spending 18 months and $20M building an in-house platform than by picking a vendor and integrating it for a quarter of the cost.
