drills.q: Monitoring vs observability in one minute?
drills.a: Monitoring checks known failure conditions with pre-aggregated signals. Observability lets you ask new questions of raw, high-cardinality events at read time. You need both: monitoring for infrastructure, observability for your own code.

drills.q: Why can't you just add user_id as a metric tag?
drills.a: Each unique tag combination becomes a new time series. Cost and query time blow up and vendors cap cardinality. Put it on events in a columnar store instead.

drills.q: Explain how a trace is assembled.
drills.a: Each span has trace ID, span ID, parent ID, start and duration. Context propagates in-process (thread-local/async context) and across processes (W3C traceparent). The backend groups spans by trace ID and builds the tree from parent IDs.

Head decides at the root using only what's known at the start: cheap, consistent, but misses errors. Tail buffers the whole trace and decides on its outcome: needs a collector tier and memory, but keeps errors and slow traces.

drills.q: How would you debug a latency spike in an unfamiliar service?
drills.a: Core analysis loop: confirm on a heatmap, select the slow band, diff dimensions against the baseline, take the strongest, filter, repeat, then look at an exemplar trace, then a profile.

Eligible: POST /checkout root spans, excluding probes. Good: status < 400 and under 4 s. Target based on business cost and dependencies (e.g. 99.9%), sliding 30-day window, short and long burn alerts.

Small error rates hide in noise, threshold and contention effects appear only at scale, aggregates smooth outliers, and samples aren't representative. Compare cohorts precisely and turn every escape into a health check.

drills.q: Your observability bill doubled. What do you do?
drills.a: Diagnose before cutting: what do we use, what's never queried, which loop are we serving? Tier fidelity, sample by key, drop unqueried data in a pipeline, attribute cost per team, and check pricing models that penalise queries.

Usually buy the backend (commodity, must be independent of your own outages), build the glue (wrappers, naming, attribution) on OTel to avoid lock-in. Price self-hosting fully: engineers, hardware, upgrades, on-call.

drills.q: How do you make an AI agent useful in incidents?
drills.a: Give it a context layer (topology, aliases, owners, recent deploys, incidents, business criticality), let it gather evidence and propose hypotheses, keep humans deciding, and measure time to understanding.

drills.q: How do you observe an LLM feature?
drills.a: OTel GenAI spans (model, tokens, prompt version, tool calls), feedback attributes, cost derived from tokens, SLOs on provider calls, promote bad traces to evals, fix the harness before rewriting prompts.

drills.q: How do you protect against AI hallucinations in a workflow that changes money?
drills.a: AI sandwich: the model emits a structured plan; a deterministic engine simulates it against invariants; reject mismatches; alert on the rejection rate; turn rejections into evals.

You don't control the environment, telemetry loss is biased toward bad sessions, workflows aren't auto-instrumentable, and bandwidth and battery matter. Use a local ring buffer, server-pushed rules, and intention → outcome SLIs by cohort.

drills.q: How do you speed up a slow CI pipeline?
drills.a: Trace it, find the critical path, check whether each step is CPU, I/O or network bound by experiment, watch P50 vs P90 for retry tax, use caches, and remember Amdahl.

drills.q: ClickHouse schema for traces: key decisions?
drills.a: Primary key matches the access path (ServiceName, Timestamp). Hot attributes as columns, the rest in Map/JSON. Bloom skip index on trace ID, materialized views for errors, TTL to S3, scale vertically before sharding.

drills.q: How would you convince leadership to change observability approach?
drills.a: Run the five tests and collect evidence, frame it as risk, capability and burden (not cost or consolidation), find the executive who owns the pain, start with one deep domain, then rerun the tests.
Accumulated misalignment between how people and process work and the technical system, e.g. developers never seeing production. AI amplifies it.

drills.q: Why are event-based SLIs better than time-sliced?
drills.a: Each request counts proportionally. A minute with 6% slow requests burns 6%, not 100%. That gives more reaction time, better accuracy for brownouts, and you can backfill SLI changes.
